43.title: Five companions
43.hook: Kondañña and four others join him in the forest near Uruvela
43.howItsDone: Buddhists take refuge in the three jewels, the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, and many practice with a community, meditating together because company makes the practice easier to keep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two teachers: Alara and Uddaka, whose deep states were good, but not the end. Your line was good, but not the end. What did you learn, and what came next? Day forty-three, and a new week: the ascetics.
screen: `TWO TEACHERS — GOOD, BUT NOT THE END.`

segments.voice: If you've ever swum laps at six in the morning, you know the regulars. The man in the blue cap. The woman who always takes the far lane. You've never learned their names. You'd never call them friends. But on a cold morning you think of them, already in the water, and you go. The wanderer has left both teachers. Now he walks on through the kingdom of Magadha until he reaches a place near the village of Uruvela: a pleasant grove, a clear river with good banks, villages nearby for alms. This, he thinks, is a good place to strive. And he isn't alone for long. Today, five companions.
screen: `THE REGULARS AT SIX A.M.` → `A GROVE NEAR URUVELA.` → `NOT ALONE FOR LONG.`

segments.voice: Five wanderers join him. Their names are Kondañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji. The later telling gives Kondañña a remarkable backstory. Remember the naming day, when the brahmins read the marks on the baby prince? Most of them said: a great king or a great teacher. The youngest said only one thing: this child will become a Buddha. That youngest brahmin was Kondañña. Now, years later, he's heard that the prince has gone forth, and he's come to find him, bringing four others. Why would five serious seekers attach themselves to this one? Because, the story says, they could see what he was: someone who wouldn't stop. They serve him, sweep, bring water, and wait. When he finds the answer, they say, he'll tell us. Hold on to them. These five will matter enormously. They'll walk away from him in anger, and they'll come back. They'll be the first people who ever hear him teach. But that's weeks away. For now, what the story shows is simple. Even this search, which is often told as one man's lonely quest, had company. Buddhism later names three treasures, and one of them is the sangha, the community of practice. Before there was a Buddha or a teaching, there was already something like a sangha: six men in a forest, keeping each other going. You don't go alone, even when it feels like you do.
screen: `FIVE NAMES.` · `KONDAÑÑA SAID IT AT THE NAMING.` · `THEY SERVE, AND WAIT.` · `A SANGHA BEFORE THE SANGHA.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T GO ALONE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Right now, somewhere, other people are doing what you're doing. A nun in Sri Lanka settling onto her mat. A nurse taking one slow breath in a hospital stairwell. Someone on a bus with their eyes closed, counting. You'll never meet them. On each of five breaths, picture one of them: five strangers on the same road, the way the five found the wanderer. Then let them go and sit with your own breath, knowing it isn't the only one being watched. The bell holds the time.
Five companions. Kondañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji: the wanderers who joined him near Uruvela, waiting for him to find the way.

Your line: you don't go alone. Today, notice one person working at something hard beside you, a coworker on the same deadline, a stranger on the same early train, and give them a nod or a word. Day forty-three.

44.title: Holding the breath
44.hook: he tries stopping the breath; his head roars like a blacksmith's bellows (MN 36)
44.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation (anapanasati), practitioners are taught not to hold or force the breath but to know it as it is, long or short; the Buddha's austerities are remembered as the path he tried and set aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five companions: Kondañña and four others, who joined him near Uruvela. Your line was you don't go alone. Who did you tell? Day forty-four.

Try to fall asleep by force. Squeeze your eyes shut. Command yourself: sleep, now. The harder you push, the more awake you get. Some things don't respond to force. The wanderer has left his two teachers, and now he tries another method of his time: the hard way. Some ascetics of his day held that if you pushed the body hard enough, through pain, hunger, stillness, the mind would break through. So he pushes. He clenches his teeth, presses his tongue to the roof of his mouth, and tries to crush his thoughts by sheer will. Sweat pours from his armpits. And then he tries something harder. Today, holding the breath.
screen: `SLEEP BY FORCE NEVER WORKS.` → `THE HARD WAY.` → `CRUSHING THOUGHT BY WILL.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this himself, years later, to a man named Saccaka. He describes what he called the breathless meditation. He stopped breathing through his mouth and nose. And when he did, he says, there was a loud roaring of winds coming out of his ears, like the roar of a blacksmith's bellows. He kept going. He stopped the breath in his ears too. And then, he says, it felt like a strong man was splitting his head with a sharp sword. Then like a tight leather strap being wound around his head. Then like a butcher carving up his belly. Then like his whole body was being roasted over hot coals. It's a hard passage to hear, and he tells it plainly. Through all of it, he says, his energy was tireless and his mindfulness was steady. He wasn't weak. He wasn't lazy. But his body, he says, was overwrought and could not calm down, worn out by the painful striving. The pain did not take over his mind. It just hurt, and it brought no breakthrough. He was forcing, and forcing wasn't finding. The breath meditation he would later teach runs almost the opposite way. In another sutta, the meditator doesn't hold the breath or push it. Breathing in long, he knows he's breathing in long. Breathing in short, he knows it's short. The breath is watched, not wrestled.
screen: `TOLD TO SACCAKA.` · `WINDS ROARING LIKE A BELLOWS.` · `STRONG EFFORT, NO BREAKTHROUGH.` · `WATCHED, NOT WRESTLED.` · then, large: `FORCING ISN'T FINDING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Take three long, easy breaths. Don't push them. Just let each one be a little slower than the last, the way a swing slows down on its own. In, and out. In, and out. In, and out. Then stop managing it altogether. Let the breath do what it wants. Long or short, deep or shallow. Your only job is to notice it. If you catch yourself controlling it, smile, and let go again. The bell holds the time.
Appanaka. The breathless meditation the wanderer forced himself through, and learned from: strong effort, great pain, no freedom.
Your line: forcing isn't finding. Today, when something won't work, a lid, a problem, a conversation, stop pushing for one breath, and see what changes. Day forty-four.

45.title: A handful of beans
45.hook: food shrinks to almost nothing; his spine shows through his belly like a string of beads (MN 36)
45.howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns eat their meals before noon under the monastic rule, eating enough to sustain practice rather than starving, and the Fasting Buddha image recalls the path the Buddha tried and set aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, appanaka, the breathless meditation: the wanderer's head roaring like a blacksmith's bellows. Your line was forcing isn't finding. Where did you stop pushing for a breath? Day forty-five.

There's a stone statue in the Lahore Museum, in Pakistan, from the old region of Gandhara. It shows a man sitting cross-legged in meditation. His face is calm. But his body is barely a body. Every rib stands out. The veins run like cords over his arms. His belly has sunk back almost to his spine. It's called the Fasting Buddha. It shows the wanderer as he would later describe himself, in the forest near Uruvela. Forcing the breath hadn't worked. So he turned to another ascetic method. Eat less. Then less. Then almost nothing. Today, a handful of beans.
screen: `A STATUE IN LAHORE.` → `EVERY RIB STANDS OUT.` → `EAT LESS. THEN ALMOST NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Again, the Buddha tells it himself, and he doesn't spare the details. He cut his food down to a handful at a time: a little bean soup, lentils, peas. And his body wasted away. His limbs, he says, became like the knotted joints of vine stems. His backside like a camel's hoof. His ribs stuck out like the rafters of an old, broken shed. The gleam of his eyes sank deep into their sockets, like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well. His scalp shriveled like a green gourd left in the sun. When he touched his belly, he could feel his spine. His spine, pressing through, looked like a string of beads. When he tried to rub his limbs, the hair fell out at the roots. People who saw him said he was black. Others said he was brown. His clear, bright skin, he says, had lost its color. Then he says the line that turns the whole story. By this painful practice, he says, I did not reach anything beyond ordinary human states. No special knowledge. No freedom. Just starvation. Why tell it in such detail? Because some ascetics of his time held that the more you denied the body, the closer you came to truth. He had tried it, and he reports back plainly: it didn't work. Starving isn't holy. In this story, the body isn't the enemy. It's where the practice happens.
screen: `A HANDFUL AT A TIME.` · `A SPINE LIKE A STRING OF BEADS.` · `NOTHING BEYOND THE ORDINARY.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `STARVING ISN'T HOLY.`

segments.voice: For this sit, picture your next meal. Or if you have something to eat nearby, take one small bite now and hold it in your mouth. Notice the taste arriving. The texture. The way the body leans toward it. Chew slowly, much more slowly than usual. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. Swallow, and feel it go down. Your body is being fed. Let that be a kindness, not a guilt. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dukkarakarika. The hard austerities of the wanderer's fasting, down to a handful of beans, and the proof, in his own words, that starving the body doesn't free the mind.
Your line: starving isn't holy. Today, eat one meal slowly, without a screen, and treat your body as a friend you're feeding. Day forty-five.

46.title: Six years
46.hook: years of hard austerity; some think he has died
46.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the six years of austerities as the extreme the Buddha tried and set aside, and teachers use them to warn against self-punishment in practice as well as against laziness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukkarakarika: the wanderer starved to a spine like a string of beads. Your line was starving isn't holy. Did you eat one meal slowly? Day forty-six.

Brave, or just stubborn? From inside a long, hard stretch, a degree that takes years, a job that can't be left, caring for someone who is ill, the two can look exactly the same. So can pushing on and being stuck. Tradition says the wanderer spent six years this way, in the forests near Uruvela. Breathless meditation. Fasting. Standing instead of sitting. Lying on a bed of thorns, by his own later account. His five companions watching, waiting. And in the later telling, one day he collapses. Today, six years.
screen: `BRAVE, OR JUST STUBBORN?` → `SIX YEARS IN THE FOREST.` → `ONE DAY HE COLLAPSES.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's own account, there's a strange moment. He says that when some gods saw him in that state, they said, the wanderer Gotama is dead. Others said, he's not dead, but he's dying. And others said, he's neither: this is simply how an awakened one lives. Nobody could tell. The later telling makes it even more vivid. He faints while walking, and falls to the ground, and a god runs to his father, King Suddhodana, with the news: your son is dead. And the old king, who had tried so hard to keep him in the palace, refuses to believe it. My son will not die, he says, before he reaches what he went looking for. Six years. The Buddha's own account in this sutta gives no number; the six years come from later tradition. But the length is the point. This wasn't a weekend. It was years of a life, given completely to one method. And the Buddha's verdict, looking back, is calm and devastating. Whatever painful feelings any ascetic has ever felt, he says, past, present or future, this was the utmost. There's none beyond it. And still, it didn't lead to awakening. Harder isn't always better. The Buddha isn't against effort. He'll later make right effort part of the path. What he's saying is that effort pointed the wrong way only digs deeper into the wrong place. A shovel works hard in a hole, too.
screen: `DEAD, DYING, OR AWAKE?` · `MY SON WILL NOT DIE YET.` · `NO ASCETIC HAD FELT MORE PAIN.` · `EFFORT POINTED THE WRONG WAY.` · then, large: `HARDER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, or even lie down if you can. Let the body be heavy. Notice where you're tired: the eyes, the back, the legs, the mind. Don't fix it. Don't push through it. Just admit it, gently, to yourself: I'm tired here. On each out-breath, let that place get a little heavier, a little more supported by the chair or the floor. You're allowed to rest. The Buddha found out the hard way. The bell holds the time.
Six years. The time tradition gives to the wanderer's austerities: pain, he says, no ascetic had gone beyond, and still not the way.
Your line: harder isn't always better. Today, when you're tired, rest for five minutes instead of pushing through, and see what the rest gives back. Day forty-six.

47.title: Remembering the rose-apple tree
47.hook: he recalls the boyhood joy under the tree: could that be the way (MN 36)
47.howItsDone: Buddhist meditation traditions teach cultivating calm joy (piti and sukha) as part of concentration, and MN 36 is read as the turn from austerity toward the way he would later teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six years: the austerities that nearly killed him, and the verdict, still not the way. Your line was harder isn't always better. Where did you rest instead of pushing? Day forty-seven.

Sometimes, when you've been stuck on a problem for hours, the answer arrives in the shower. Or on a walk. Or right as you're falling asleep. Not from pushing harder. From somewhere you'd stopped looking. The wanderer has reached the end of the hard way. The breath, the fasting, the pain: he has pushed each one as far as it goes, and none of it has worked. So he sits, thin as a shadow, and asks: could there be another way to awakening? And a memory comes back, the one we heard on day twenty-seven. This time, not the memory itself, but what it did to him. Today, remembering the rose-apple tree.
screen: `THE ANSWER IN THE SHOWER.` → `THE END OF THE HARD WAY.` → `A MEMORY FROM CHILDHOOD.`

segments.voice: On day twenty-seven we stood in the shade with the boy. Today we're with the man, and the same memory lands very differently. In the Buddha's account, it comes in three steps. First, the memory: once, while his father the Sakyan was working, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind settled into the first jhana, a calm, secluded joy. Second, a question: could that be the path to awakening? Third, the answer, which he says came right after the memory: that is the path. Look at where he's sitting when this happens. Not in a palace, not as a beginner, but at the far end of years of hardship, with everything he's built his search on in pieces. He has been treating ease as the enemy. And now he asks himself, why am I afraid of that happiness, a happiness that has nothing to do with sensual pleasure or anything unwholesome? I'm not afraid of it, he answers. That's a reversal. The clue had been sitting in his own past the whole time, while he looked for the answer in pain. And then comes the hard, practical part. He looks at his body, all bones, and he says it plainly: it isn't easy to reach that kind of joy with a body this worn out. So, he decides, I will eat some solid food. The memory doesn't just comfort him. It changes his plan. The joy was a clue, and following a clue means doing something different tomorrow.
screen: `THE MAN, NOT THE BOY.` · `MEMORY, QUESTION, ANSWER.` · `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT JOY?` · `NOT IN THIS BODY. I WILL EAT.` · then, large: `THE JOY WAS A CLUE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Now remember a moment of easy calm from this past week. Not a big event. A small one. A quiet minute with a cup of something hot. Sunlight across a floor. A walk where nothing needed doing. Let the memory come back with its details: the temperature, the sounds, the smell. Then ask it, the way he asked his: what were the conditions? What was absent, what was present, that let the calm come? Don't force an answer. Just notice whatever the body does with the remembering. The bell holds the time.
Jambu. The rose-apple tree under which the wanderer recalled a calm joy from boyhood, and realized it pointed the way.
Your line: the joy was a clue. Today, when a small moment of calm shows up, don't hurry past it. Stay with it for three breaths, and notice what made room for it. Day forty-seven.

48.title: Sujata's bowl of rice
48.hook: a village woman offers milk-rice; he eats, and the five leave him in disgust
48.howItsDone: Offering food to monks and nuns is one of the most common Buddhist practices, and many Buddhists remember Sujata's gift; in some places people make milk-rice offerings on Vesak in her memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jambu, the rose-apple tree: a calm joy from boyhood that pointed the way. Your line was the joy was a clue. Did you stay with a small calm moment? Day forty-eight.

Someone has probably made you a meal when you needed it more than you knew. A friend who showed up after a funeral with a casserole. A grandmother who wouldn't let you leave without eating. A stranger who bought you lunch. Food given at the right moment can feel like being brought back to life. The wanderer has made his decision. To reach the calm he remembered from the rose-apple tree, he needs a body that can sit. So he's going to eat. Real food. And in the village of Senani, near Uruvela, there lives a young woman named Sujata, who has been preparing a very special bowl of rice. Today, Sujata's bowl of rice.
screen: `A MEAL WHEN YOU NEEDED IT.` → `HE DECIDES TO EAT.` → `A YOUNG WOMAN NAMED SUJATA.`

segments.voice: This meal comes to us from two places, an old one and a later one. In the Buddha's own account, he simply says: I ate solid food, rice and bread. And my five companions, who had been waiting for me to find the truth, were disgusted. They said: the wanderer Gotama has become self-indulgent. He's given up the struggle. And they left him. The later telling gives the meal a face. Sujata, the telling says, had once made a vow at a banyan tree: if she married well and had a son, she would bring an offering to the spirit of that tree. Her wish came true. So she prepared the richest milk-rice she could, and sent her servant ahead to clean the place. The servant saw the thin wanderer sitting under the banyan, glowing in the early light, and ran back: the tree spirit has come in person! Sujata came with a golden bowl of milk-rice and offered it to him. He accepted, and ate. Think about who she is in the story. Not a queen, not a priest, not a famous teacher. A young mother from a village, keeping a promise. And her bowl gives him the strength for everything that comes next. That's why Buddhists honor her to this day, and why some remember her as one of the Buddha's first supporters. And the five? By the morning of Sujata's bowl they're already gone, sure he's failed. It's one of the story's quiet ironies. The people waiting for him to succeed left just before he did.
screen: `RICE AND BREAD. THE FIVE LEAVE.` · `A VOW AT A BANYAN TREE.` · `THE TREE SPIRIT HAS COME!` · `A YOUNG MOTHER FEEDS THE WAY.` · then, large: `FEED THE ONE WHO WALKS.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, hold it. If not, picture the last thing you ate. Before anything else, just look at it. Think of the people behind it: someone who grew it, someone who carried it, someone who cooked it or packed it. Silently thank them. Then take one slow bite or sip. Let it be a gift received, the way the wanderer received Sujata's bowl. Notice the strength it gives, even a little. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Payasa. The milk-rice Sujata offered the starving wanderer, which gave him strength for the night ahead.
Your line: feed the one who walks. Today, eat something with thanks, and if you can, feed someone else who's on a long road. Day forty-eight.

49.title: The bowl upstream
49.hook: a later telling: he sets the bowl on the river; if it floats upstream he will awaken, and it does
49.howItsDone: The bowl floating upstream appears in Buddhist temple murals, including in Thailand, and teachers use it to picture the dharma as going against the stream of craving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, payasa, Sujata's gift of milk-rice: a village woman's gift, and the five walking away. Your line was feed the one who walks. What did you eat with thanks? Day forty-nine, the end of the week of the ascetics.

If the light turns green before I get there, it's a sign. If the next song is our song, I'll call. People make small bargains like these with the world when something big is on their minds, half joking, half hoping. The wanderer has eaten Sujata's milk-rice. He's bathed in the river Neranjara. The telling says he's holding the empty golden bowl, standing at the water's edge. Tonight, he senses, is the night. And he does something that looks a lot like our little bargains, except the stakes are everything. Today, the bowl upstream.
screen: `IF THE LIGHT TURNS GREEN...` → `THE EMPTY GOLDEN BOWL.` → `AT THE WATER'S EDGE.`

segments.voice: This comes from the later telling, not the suttas. He sets the bowl on the river and says: if I'm going to become a Buddha today, let this bowl float upstream. If not, let it go with the current. And the bowl turns, and floats against the flow of the river, straight upstream, a long way, the story says, and then sinks. And the telling adds one more detail. It sinks down to the palace of a serpent king under the river, and lands with a little click against three other bowls: the bowls of three Buddhas who came before. Now, why this image? A river is a plain picture of the way things usually go. Downstream. Gravity. Habit. And in a sutta, the Buddha describes what he found as going against the stream: subtle, deep, hard to see for people who delight in clinging. The word for someone who has entered the path is sotapanna, a stream-enterer, which pictures the path itself as a river running toward freedom. So the bowl floating upstream can be read as the teaching in one picture: what he's about to find moves against the flow of wanting. And look back at this week: five companions, the breath held till his head roared, dukkarakarika, six years, jambu, Sujata's bowl, and now this one. Again and again, the hard way failed, and something gentler pointed forward.
screen: `IF I'LL AWAKEN, GO UPSTREAM.` · `A CLICK AGAINST THREE BOWLS.` · `A TEACHING THAT GOES UPSTREAM.` · `THE HARD WAY FAILED.` · then, large: `AGAINST THE CURRENT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one hope you've been holding tightly. Something you want to happen. A result, a reply, a change. Picture setting it on a river, the way the wanderer set down his bowl. You're not giving up on it. You're just not clutching it anymore. Watch it float. Where it goes is not entirely up to you. Feel your hands, empty now, resting in your lap. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Neranjara. The river where, in the later telling, the wanderer set his golden bowl, which floated upstream against the current as a sign he would awaken.
Your line: against the current. Today, notice one habit that runs downstream, and set down one hope gently instead of gripping it. Day forty-nine.

original.note: Pali: the river Neranjara, near Uruvela, where the Buddha bathed on the day of his awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic bowl floated the wrong way.
what it means: the image pictures the Buddha's teaching itself: moving against the current of wanting.
what a scholar hears: the bowl story is from the Nidanakatha (the bowl sinks to the naga king Kala's realm); MN 26 calls the dhamma paṭisotagāmi, going against the stream.
